## What is slow

**GET /dispatch** (frontend) is the only endpoint in the steady state: **p50 375.7 ms, p95 472.2 ms, 5% failures** (2 of 40 traces).

## Why it is slow — the critical path

The slowest request (511 ms) waits on this chain, and the latency owners are:

| Owner | Share | Per request | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| **redis-manual `GetDriver`** | **49.9%** | 188.8 ms | Simulated Redis GET with random timeouts; called once per driver, retried on error |
| **mysql `SQL SELECT`** | 25.3% | 95.9 ms | Simulated MySQL: a mutex serialises connections + fixed query delay |
| **route `GET /route`** | 17.7% | 66.8 ms | CPU-bound route computation per call |
| redis-manual `FindDriverIDs` | 5.6% | 21.3 ms | Simulated Redis scan |

### The two amplifiers

1. **Fan-out to redis-manual: 13.1 calls per request** (driver → redis-manual). Every `GetDriver` call is on the critical path, so the fan-out multiplies the Redis cost.
2. **Silent retries:** 94 failed `GetDriver` calls were retried across 33 requests, wasting **75.9 ms per request**, and **all 94 retries land on the critical path**. The trace shows repeated `GetDriver` spans alternating success/failure (13.6 ms ok → 31.3 ms error → 12.9 ms ok …).

### The structural issues

- **mysql** serialises all connections behind a mutex, so the 95.9 ms/query is a fixed contention cost, not network.
- **frontend → route** also fans out **9.5 calls per request** through a worker pool whose HTTP client has no short timeout.
- **No redundancy:** every path to `/dispatch` runs through customer, driver, redis-manual, route, and mysql — pausing any one fails all 40 requests.

In short: half the latency is Redis `GetDriver` (slow + retried + fanned out 13x), a quarter is the mutex-serialized MySQL query, and ~18% is CPU-bound route computation fanned out ~9.5x.

**What to break next:** `driver` — it's the top-ranked untested target (priority 0.712). The graph predicts stopping it breaks 100% of requests (blast radius 100%, betweenness 2, 40 inbound calls). It has never been paused in an experiment, so there's no prior verdict to skip.

**What the last experiment taught us:**

The last experiment (`exp-0708eb20`) paused `customer` and was **CONFIRMED**:

- **Failure mode:** `GET /dispatch` did not fail fast — p50 jumped from 1209 ms baseline to 35002 ms when `customer` stopped.
- **Lesson:** A timeout or circuit breaker on the hop into `customer` would turn a hang into an error instead of a 30+ second block.
- **Backlog lesson:** 6 calls into `mysql` ran after `customer` resumed, after every caller had already given up — no deadline reached the callee, so the work ran late for nobody.

The two prior experiments (`route` and `customer`) both taught the same core lesson: hops hang instead of failing, and timeouts/circuit breakers are the fix. Guardrails have already been proposed for `frontend -> customer` (450 ms timeout) and `frontend -> route` (250 ms timeout), both marked high priority.
